name: Bafut
confidence_why: Nothing read describes word stress in Bafut itself: Anderson 2001 only suggests root-initial stress for Eastern Grassfields languages as a family, illustrated from Ngiemboon, and Mfonyam 1989, the one large Bafut phonology available, says nothing about Bafut stress while noting that the sister language Mankon does not seem to be a stress-accent language, so whether Bafut has word stress at all, and where, is unknown.
catalog_citation: Mfonyam, Joseph Ngwa. 1989. Tone in orthography: the case of Bafut and related languages. Thèse de Doctorat d'État, Université de Yaoundé. xvi+686 pp. (open via CORE 210667367 / MPG PuRe)
catalog_locator: ch. 4 'Tone System', §4.0 'Introduction' and §4.1 'Level Tones' of the 668-page CORE scan (page-foot number scan-read '49', preceding page '47'; i.e. p. 48/49). Mankon remark: pp. 393-394.
catalog_quote: 4.0 Introduction The functional load of tone in Bafut is very significant. Tone plays an important role both at the lexical and grammatical levels in the language. [...] 4.1 Level Tones There are three level (register) phonemic tones in Bafut. H (high), M (mid) and L (low). The three phonemic tones in Bafut have developed from an underlying two tone system. In addition to thc three phonemic tones in Bafut, there is a downstepped high tone ('H) which is different from the phonemic mid tone. This will be treated in more detail in 4.4 and 4.5. The three phonemic tones are marked as indicated below: (1) H kaa "crab" [...]

new_statements.quote: Stress phenomena have gone largely unmentioned in most descriptions of Bantoid languages (and Eastern Grassfields languages are no exception). This author feels that the reason for this is that amplitude phenomena in these languages are mostly predictable, perhaps to compensate for the complexity of its tonal phenomena (see section 8.3 below). 6.1 Nouns and Verbs: First syllable of root. For nouns and verbs with single roots, it appears that the first syllable of the root is stressed. This means that all noun and verb prefixes and any second syllables on the roots are unstressed. In addition to less amplitude, these unstressed syllables often are more predictable than the stressed syllables
new_statements.citation: Anderson, Stephen C. 2001. Phonological characteristics of Eastern Grassfields languages. In N. M. Mutaka & S. B. Chumbow (eds.), Research Mate in African Linguistics: Focus on Cameroon (GAAS 17), Köln: Köppe. Section 6 'Stress', p. 47.
new_statements.locator: printed p. 47 (archive.org leaf 63), section 6 'Stress', 6.1 'Nouns and Verbs: First syllable of root'; scope statement listing 'Ngemba (Bafut, Mankon, Bambili, Nkwen, Pinyin, Awing, etc.)' on p. 33
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote check: the Anderson 2001 passage is present verbatim in the saved scanned text at lines 3377-3387, under the running head 'Phonology of Eastern Grassfields languages 47', section '6. Stress' and '6.1 Nouns and Verbs: First syllable of root'. The quote stops mid-sentence; the source continues '(e.g. lack of tone contrast for noun class prefixes and predictable "echo vowels" at the end of certain roots)', then 6.2 Functors ('it seems likely that most functors will lack stress.. certain functors may receive stress (e.g. contrastive focus)'), matching the compiler secondary/exceptions notes. Scope: line 2433 (printed p. 33) lists 'Ngemba (Bafut, Mankon, Bambili, Nkwen, Pinyin, Awing, etc.…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Genus-level generalization for Eastern Grassfields Bantu (explicitly including the Ngemba group with Bafut): in nouns and verbs the root-initial syllable carries stress (greater amplitude); noun-class/verb prefixes and any second root syllable are unstressed. NOT a Bafut-specific description; the author's examples are from Ngiemboon and the claim is hedged ('it appears').
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; functors said to probably lack stress except under contrastive focus (6.2).
new_statements.exceptions: Functors may receive stress under contrastive focus; otherwise 'awaits future research'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (root-initial) impressionistic amplitude prominence in a tone language; family-level claim, not verified for Bafut. The accessible Bafut-specific description (Mfonyam 1989, 686 pp., tone/intonation) is silent on word stress; it only notes a falling intonation contour on the final syllable of citation forms (p. 100) and, for sister-language Mankon, that it 'does not seem to be a stress accent language' (pp. 393-394). Tamanji 2009's reference grammar (ch. 1 'The Sound System') could contain a Bafut-specific statement but was not accessible.
new_statements.identity_note: All Bafut-specific sources describe the central Bafut variety (bafu1246, ISO bfd; Ngemba subgroup of Mbam-Nkam/Eastern Grassfields). The only stress statement found (Anderson 2001) is a genus-level generalization for Eastern Grassfields exemplified from Ngiemboon (ngie1241), not from Bafut; Mfonyam's 'not a stress accent language' remark concerns Mankon (mank1253), Bafut's closest sister.

sources.note: Identifies three tone processes in Bafut nouns - Tone Lowering (TL), High Tone Spread (HTS) and Phrase-Final L Tone Docking (PFLTD) - and classifies nouns by tonal behaviour: TL affects the first syllable only vs two or more syllables; HTS yields nouns with a surface high-falling contour on the first syllable, a surface H there, or downstepped H on all syllables; PFLTD yields utterance-final L vs final H; behaviour depends on whether the noun is lexically toneless, H-toned or L-toned and whether the stem is HH or H; patterns read as residue of Grassfields Bantu historical tone changes.

tone.summary: Lexical H vs L vs toneless nouns; downstepped H; surface HL falling contour from H tone spread; floating/phrase-final L docking (abstract only).
